extracted.intended_audience: educational institutions (Title IX coordinators, administrators), institutional legal counsel, compliance officers
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and operationalize the Department of Education's regulatory definition(s) and enforcement standards for sex-based harassment under Title IX, including quid pro quo, hostile environment, and related procedural safeguards. Includes guidance on scope, vagueness/overbreadth concerns, First Amendment interactions, and evidentiary/grievance protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct must be 'on the basis of sex'
rubrics_metrics.description: The conduct prohibited must be 'on the basis of sex' and the definition includes sexual harassment and harassment on the bases described in §106.10. 'On the basis of sex' does not require that the conduct be sexual in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains that Title IX's prohibition encompasses discrimination based on sex stereotypes, sex characteristics, pregnancy or related conditions, sexual orientation, and gender identity—each of which depends at least in part on consideration of a person's sex. Harassing acts that are verbal, nonverbal, or physical aggression, intimidation, or hostility based on sex may fall within Title IX if they meet the regulatory definition. Coverage may include online conduct as well as in-person conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex-based harassment comprises sexual harassment and other harassment on the basis of sex (including §106.10 bases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex-based harassment 'means sexual harassment and other harassment on the basis of sex, including on the bases described in §106.10.' The three categories of harassment (quid pro quo, hostile environment, or specific offenses) modify 'sexual harassment and other harassment on the basis of sex.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department changed proposed wording to 'other harassment on the basis of sex' to align clearly with §106.10 and to tie the three categories directly to both sexual harassment and other sex-based harassment. To constitute prohibited sex-based harassment, the sexual harassment or harassment on the bases described in §106.10 must satisfy one or more of the three categories (quid pro quo, hostile environment, or specific offenses). The Department declined to further define 'harassment' beyond these categories, finding the definition sufficiently clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hostile environment: unwelcome, sex-based, subjective and objective offensiveness, and severe or pervasive impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Hostile environment sex-based harassment is required to be unwelcome, sex-based, subjectively and objectively offensive, and so severe or pervasive that the conduct results in a limitation or denial of a person's ability to participate in or benefit from the recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final definition explicitly requires both subjective and objective offensiveness and that the conduct be 'severe or pervasive' (note: the Department uses 'severe or pervasive' rather than the Davis phrasing 'severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive'). The regulation also 'enumerates the factors that a recipient must, at a minimum, consider' when determining whether a hostile environment has been created (those specific factors are discussed elsewhere in the rule). This framing is intended to target discriminatory conduct with an impact greater than merely being bothersome or offensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with Davis standard (administrative vs private damages contexts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department's regulatory definition of hostile environment is consistent with the Davis standard in requiring a contextual totality-of-circumstances analysis about whether harassment impacted educational benefits, but differs in formulation because administrative enforcement has different goals than private damages actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Davis addressed the standard for private money-damages suits ('severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive'); the Department explains that Davis's phrasing was meant for private damages contexts and that an administrative enforcement standard may appropriately differ. The Department asserts its final definition still implicates access to educational programs and is compatible with Davis while adopting regulatory guardrails suited to administrative enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of subjective and objective standards to avoid vagueness/overbreadth
rubrics_metrics.description: A hostile environment requires both subjective and objective offensiveness; inclusion of an 'objective' qualifier and similar limiting language provides adequate notice and narrows policies so they are not void for vagueness or overbroad under the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department cites case law (e.g., Rowles, Koeppel, Vanderhurst, Marshall) to support that objective and subjective standards are understood in common usage and help recipients and individuals know what conduct is prohibited. The rule adopts these longstanding standards and rejects calls to define many additional 'key terms,' finding the current approach sufficiently clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quid pro quo harassment: scope and elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Quid pro quo sex-based harassment covers any employee, agent, or other person authorized by the recipient to provide an aid, benefit, or service under the recipient's education program or activity and includes both explicit and implied conditioning of such aid/benefit/service on a person's participation in sexual conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declines to remove 'unwelcome' from quid pro quo, explaining unwelcomeness is a well-established component of harassment law; acquiescence does not imply the conduct was welcome. 'Other person authorized by the recipient' includes teaching assistants, volunteer coaches, board members (paid or unpaid), and others authorized to provide an aid/benefit/service—but does not list students generally (students would be covered only if they occupy an authorized role). Quid pro quo can cover conditioning academic and non-academic aids/benefits (including extracurriculars), and threats of detriment are covered even if the threat is not carried out. The Department confirms implied conditioning is included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguards to mitigate false allegations concerns in grievance procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Final regulations incorporate procedural safeguards to address false-allegation concerns, including evaluation based on all relevant not otherwise impermissible evidence, equal opportunity to access relevant evidence or receive an accurate description, processes to question parties and witnesses when credibility is in dispute, and reasonable steps to protect privacy during grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific regulatory citations: evaluation based on relevant evidence (§106.45(b)(6) and (7)); equal opportunity to access relevant evidence or receive an accurate description (§106.45(f)(4)); process to question parties/witnesses where credibility is in dispute (§106.45(g)); steps to protect privacy while grievance procedures are pending (§106.45(b)(5)). The rules permit disciplining individuals who make false statements provided discipline is not imposed solely based on the recipient's determination whether sex discrimination occurred (§106.45(h)(5)). These measures are cited as mitigating the risk of meritless investigations and inconsistent enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment considerations and limits on regulating speech
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department's definition is crafted with the First Amendment in mind: it aims at discriminatory conduct (unwelcome, sex-based, and subjectively and objectively offensive, and severe or pervasive) rather than content-based regulation of speech, and recipients retain discretion in how to remedy hostile environments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes that even if a rule aimed at offensive conduct impacts speech in some circumstances, it does not necessarily become vague or overbroad; courts have upheld similar conduct-focused policies. The rule points to additional First Amendment discussion elsewhere in the regulation and emphasizes that recipients have multiple means to remedy hostile environments and remain free to decide whether discipline is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual harassment as subset defined by the three categories
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'sexual harassment' in the definition refers to conduct that constitutes quid pro quo harassment, hostile environment harassment, or a specific offense listed in the definition of 'sex-based harassment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As explained in prior OCR guidance, sexual harassment can include unwelcome sexual advances, requests for sexual favors, and other verbal, nonverbal, or physical conduct of a sexual nature. The Department declined to remove an explicit reference to 'sexual harassment' in the introductory sentence so as to explicitly include both sexual and non-sexual forms of sex-based harassment (e.g., based on pregnancy, gender identity, sex stereotypes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Online conduct included within hostile environment coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Harassing conduct that occurs online, in addition to in person, can constitute hostile environment sex-based harassment if it otherwise meets the regulatory requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes that covered conduct could occur online and refers readers to the section on Hostile Environment Sex-Based Harassment—Online Harassment (§106.2) for further discussion.
